newsitem.title: USA: Republican panel leader sees no anti-Gingrich move.
newsitem.headline: Republican panel leader sees no anti-Gingrich move.

text.p: The chairman of the Republican Congressional Campaign Committee said Tuesday that he saw no sign of a coordinated effort by party members to oppose Newt Gingrich's re-election as speaker of the House.

In recent days, a few Republican House members have called publicly on Gingrich to step aside because of ethics allegations against him. But Representative John Linder, a fellow Georgia Republican and the party congressional committee's chairman, said there was no "groundswell" of opposition.

Linder said House Republicans who doubt the speaker's ability to lead should keep quiet. "It's somewhat unseemly for our members to have come through a tough election and won, and then to attack their own leadership," he said in an interview broadcast on local radio.

He dismissed suggestions that Gingrich simply step aside until the House Ethics Committee completes its probe of his activities, saying Democrats would never tire of filing new charges against him. "This is an effort to destroy Speaker Gingrich and they're going to continue," he said, terming the House ethics process "a political tool."

The panel is investigating whether a televised college course Gingrich taught used tax-deductible charitable contributions improperly for political purposes. He also faces allegations of improperly receiving gifts and campaign contributions from GOPAC, a Republican political action committee he once headed.

On Sunday, Representative Steve Largent, a Republican from Oklahoma, said Gingrich should hand the gavel over to a colleague, perhaps Representative Henry Hyde of Illinois, in order to reduce the volume of political rhetoric in the House.
New York Republican Representative Peter King told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution on Tuesday that Gingrich should "step aside for the good of the country and the good of the party."

The newspaper also quoted Representative Christopher Shays of Connecticut as saying he could not support Gingrich's re-election as speaker in January unless the formal ethics complaints were resolved.
House Republicans were expected to nominate leaders of the next Congress in a Nov. 20 caucus.
Linder, who spoke to Largent by telephone after Sunday's television appearance, said the Oklahoma Republican was sorry for his remarks about Gingrich.
